gbm_evidence: None found. Targeted searches for LARP1 in glioma/glioblastoma returned no primary study of LARP1 itself in glioma. The closest hits are (a) a different family member - 'Identification of RNA-Binding Protein LARP4B as a Tumor Suppressor in Glioma' (Cancer Res 2016), which is LARP4B not LARP1 and points in the opposite direction, and (b) an RSK1/RSK2 translatome study in glioblastoma cells (Neuro-Oncology Advances 2025) in which LARP1 appears as pathway context rather than as the studied target. Reported honestly as no GBM-specific evidence.
subtype_link: INT has no single defining programme, so subtype-specificity is not really assessable. Programme assignment: LARP1 belongs to the mTORC1-controlled cap-dependent translation / ribosome-biogenesis programme. This is a general growth programme present across all GBM subtypes and is in no way INT-specific; there is no published basis for assigning it to an intermediate state rather than to any other.
druggable: Indirectly. No selective LARP1 inhibitor was found. The tractable node is upstream: mTOR kinase inhibitors (everolimus, temsirolimus - approved in other oncology indications; rapalogs have been trialled in GBM without success) and mTOR-kinase inhibitors control LARP1 phosphorylation. Approval status for direct LARP1 targeting: none known.
cancer_relevance: Yes, reasonably solid. 'LARP1 post-transcriptionally regulates mTOR and contributes to cancer progression' (Oncogene 2015); 'The RNA-binding protein LARP1 is a post-transcriptional regulator of survival and tumorigenesis in ovarian cancer' (PMID 26717985); 'Overexpression of LARP1 predicts poor prognosis of colorectal cancer and is expected to be a potential therapeutic target' (Tumor Biology 2016); more recent work implicates it in AML translation/metabolism and breast cancer prognosis and immune microenvironment.
drug_detail: No selective LARP1 inhibitor. The tractable node is upstream — mTOR inhibitors. Rapalogs have been trialled in GBM WITHOUT success.

protein_function: Poly(A)-specific ribonuclease, a 3'-to-5' deadenylase that trims mRNA poly(A) tails and performs the 3'-end maturation of non-coding RNAs including the telomerase RNA component TERC.
gbm_evidence: Yes, strong and direct. Yin J, Seo Y, Rhim J, et al. 'Cross-talk between PARN and EGFR-STAT3 Signaling Facilitates Self-Renewal and Proliferation of Glioblastoma Stem Cells.' Cancer Research 2023;83(22):3693-3709 (PMID 37747775). Key findings: 'A positive feedback loop comprising PARN and EGFR-STAT3 signaling supports self-renewal and proliferation of glioblastoma stem cells'; PARN expression correlated with poor patient survival, and 'PARN depletion in GSCs reduced infiltration and prolonged survival' in vivo. The authors propose the network as a therapeutic target in GBM. Source: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/37747775/
subtype_link: INT has no single defining programme, so subtype-specificity is largely not assessable. Programme assignment: PARN belongs to RNA 3'-end processing / mRNA turnover and telomere-maintenance (TERC maturation). It is NOT INT-specific - notably, the published GBM work ties PARN to EGFR-STAT3 signalling and stem-cell self-renewal, which are programmes conventionally associated with the classical (EGFR-amplified) and mesenchymal/STAT3 axes rather than with an intermediate state. So the gene has real GBM credentials but its assignment to INT specifically is not supported by evidence; it would be equally or better placed elsewhere.
druggable: Weakly. No approved or clinical-stage PARN inhibitor was found. Nucleotide-analogue and small-molecule PARN inhibitors exist only as early research tools in the enzymology literature; the GBM study used genetic depletion. Approval status: preclinical / none known.
cancer_relevance: Moderate, and directionally mixed. PARN biallelic loss-of-function causes dyskeratosis congenita and pulmonary fibrosis via impaired TERC 3'-end maturation and telomere shortening (Nat Genet 2015, JCI 2015), i.e. germline loss is pathogenic. In somatic cancer the GBM stem-cell paper above is the clearest oncogenic-dependency evidence.
drug_detail: No approved or clinical-stage PARN inhibitor. Inhibitors exist only as early research tools; the glioblastoma study used genetic depletion.
tier: TIER 2 · credible target, no drug yet

protein_function: Type I-alpha regulatory subunit of protein kinase A, which binds and holds the PKA catalytic subunits inactive until cAMP binding releases them; it is therefore the principal brake on cAMP/PKA signalling.
gbm_evidence: Essentially none direct. The only glioma-adjacent finding is Guo et al. (PMID 30536597), 'Glioma exosomes mediate the expansion and function of myeloid-derived suppressor cells through microRNA-29a/Hbp1 and microRNA-92a/Prkar1a pathways' - here glioma-derived exosomal miR-92a suppresses Prkar1a in MYELOID cells (MDSCs), not in the tumour cells, so this is a microenvironmental observation rather than evidence of PRKAR1A as a tumour-intrinsic glioma gene. No study of PRKAR1A expression, mutation or dependency in GBM tumour cells was found. Source: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/30536597/
subtype_link: INT is explicitly the least well-defined of the six subtypes and has no single dominant programme, so subtype-specificity is not really assessable here. Programme assignment: PRKAR1A belongs to cAMP/PKA second-messenger signalling, a housekeeping-adjacent regulatory programme, not to any recognised GBM lineage or immune module. There is no evidence it is INT-specific. Of note, Prkar1a deletion has been shown to drive a MESENCHYMAL-to-epithelial transition (PMC3129546), which if anything argues against a mesenchymal assignment and is a weak, indirect point in favour of it not belonging in MES.
druggable: FLAG - WRONG THERAPEUTIC DIRECTION. PRKAR1A is a well-established TUMOUR SUPPRESSOR: germline inactivating mutations cause Carney complex (GeneReviews), and Sandrini et al. (Genes Chromosomes Cancer 2002) describe it explicitly as 'Regulatory subunit type I-alpha of protein kinase A (PRKAR1A): A tumor-suppressor gene for sporadic thyroid cancer'; an expressed PRKAR1A mutation is associated with aggressive tumours (Cancer Res 2008). Inhibiting PRKAR1A would RELEASE PKA catalytic activity and phenocopy the oncogenic lesion, so an inhibitor would be actively counterproductive. There are cAMP-analogue PKA modulators and PKA catalytic-subunit inhibitors (H-89, PKI peptide) as research tools only - none approved, and none of them target PRKAR1A in the correct direction. Approval status: none known.
cancer_relevance: Yes, as a tumour suppressor. Loss-of-function underlies Carney complex (myxomas, primary pigmented nodular adrenocortical disease, schwannomas, thyroid and testicular tumours); PRKAR1A mutations also occur in sporadic cardiac myxomas and sporadic thyroid cancer. The oncogenic driver in this axis is loss of PRKAR1A, i.e. PKA hyperactivity.
drug_detail: FLAG - WRONG THERAPEUTIC DIRECTION. PRKAR1A is a well-established TUMOUR SUPPRESSOR: germline inactivating mutations cause Carney complex (GeneReviews), and Sandrini et al. (Genes Chromosomes Cancer 2002) describe it explicitly as 'Regulatory subunit type I-alpha of protein kinase A (PRKAR1A): A tumor-suppressor gene for sporadic thyroid cancer'; an expressed PRKAR1A mutation is associated with aggressive tumours (Cancer Res 2008). Inhibiting PRKAR1A would RELEASE PKA catalytic activity and phenocopy the oncogenic lesion, so an inhibitor would be actively counterproductive. There are cAMP-analogue PKA modulators and PKA catalytic-subunit inhibitors (H-89, PKI peptide) as research tools only - none approved, and none of them target PRKAR1A in the correct direction. Approval status: none known.
wrong_direction: TUMOUR SUPPRESSOR. Germline inactivating mutations cause Carney complex; described as a tumour-suppressor gene for sporadic thyroid cancer. Inhibiting it would remove a brake on growth.

protein_function: Endoplasmic reticulum membrane protein of the Sec61 translocon accessory complex (with Sec63) that mediates post-translational protein translocation into the ER and contributes to ER calcium leakage and recovery from ER stress (recovER-phagy).
gbm_evidence: None found. Targeted searches returned no primary study of SEC62 in glioma or glioblastoma. The Human Protein Atlas lists SEC62 as prognostic only in head and neck (unfavourable), ovarian (unfavourable), pancreatic (unfavourable) and renal (favourable) cancer, and for glioblastoma reports the survival association as 'Non-significant'; protein staining shows only that 'A few gliomas ... displayed strong positivity'. Note the frequently co-retrieved GBM papers concern SEC61G, a different gene ('SEC61G assists EGFR-amplified glioblastoma to evade immune elimination', PNAS 2023) - that evidence must not be credited to SEC62. Sources: http://www.proteinatlas.org/ENSG00000008952-SEC62/pathology/glioma ; https://www.pnas.org/doi/10.1073/pnas.2303400120
subtype_link: None found. INT has no single defining programme, so subtype-specificity is not assessable; SEC62 belongs to ER protein translocation, ER stress tolerance and calcium homeostasis. There is no published link to any GBM subtype and no basis for calling it INT-specific.
druggable: Partially, tool-compound level. Trifluoperazine, a calmodulin antagonist and approved antipsychotic, is reported to antagonise Sec62 function: it 'phenocopied the effect of SEC62-targeting siRNAs' by suppressing stress tolerance and migratory potential in SEC62-overexpressing tumour cells (Frontiers in Physiology 2022). Mycalamide A and related compounds inhibit the Sec61 translocon more broadly. Approval status: trifluoperazine is approved as an antipsychotic but NOT approved or in trials for this indication; SEC62 targeting is preclinical.
cancer_relevance: Yes, reasonably well developed. SEC62 is amplified at 3q26 and over-expressed in prostate, non-small cell lung, thyroid, hepatocellular, breast, head and neck, cervical, ovarian, gastric, vulvar cancer and melanoma; 'Silencing of the SEC62 gene inhibits migratory and invasive potential of various tumor cells' (PMID 20669223) establishes a functional pro-migratory role.
drug_detail: Trifluoperazine, an approved antipsychotic, antagonises Sec62 function in cell studies. Not a developed oncology agent.

protein_function: Protection of telomeres 1, the single-stranded-DNA-binding subunit of the six-protein shelterin complex that caps the telomeric 3' overhang, suppresses the ATR-dependent DNA damage response at chromosome ends, and restricts telomerase access.
gbm_evidence: Yes, and it is glioma-specific germline evidence. Bainbridge MN et al. (Gliogene Consortium), 'Germline Mutations in Shelterin Complex Genes Are Associated With Familial Glioma', JNCI 2015;107(1):dju384 (PMID 25482530), identified germline POT1 mutations segregating with disease across familial glioma pedigrees; a companion commentary, 'POT1: a genetic link for familial glioma' (PMID 25524796), makes the association explicit. GeneReviews 'POT1 Tumor Predisposition' lists gliomas among the core tumours of the syndrome: 'Multiple cutaneous melanomas, sarcomas (particularly cardiac angiosarcomas), chronic lymphocytic leukemia (CLL), and gliomas.' Sources: https://academic.oup.com/jnci/article-abstract/107/1/dju384/912413 ; https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/25482530/ ; https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK563529/
subtype_link: INT has no single defining programme, so subtype-specificity is not assessable. Programme assignment: POT1 belongs to telomere maintenance / genome stability. Critically, the glioma evidence is GERMLINE PREDISPOSITION, not subtype-restricted somatic biology, and nothing in the literature links POT1 to an intermediate or transitional GBM cell state. It is not INT-specific in any documented sense.
druggable: FLAG - WRONG THERAPEUTIC DIRECTION. POT1 is a TUMOUR SUPPRESSOR. GeneReviews states the mechanism explicitly: 'Loss of function. Haploinsufficiency is the proposed underlying mechanism for overall telomere lengthening and the resulting fragile and dysfunctional telomeres.' Pathogenic germline variants are loss-of-function and predispose to glioma, melanoma, angiosarcoma and CLL. Inhibiting POT1 would therefore phenocopy the cancer-predisposing lesion and is the wrong therapeutic direction. No POT1 inhibitor is known; the plausible therapeutic angle in POT1-mutant tumours is synthetic-lethal exploitation of telomere dysfunction (e.g. ATR inhibitors), which is a separate hypothesis and not POT1 targeting. Approval status: none known.
cancer_relevance: Extensive, as a predisposition gene. POT1 germline variants define a hereditary cancer syndrome spanning melanoma, cardiac and non-cardiac angiosarcoma, CLL, glioma, thyroid cancer and others; somatic POT1 mutations recur in CLL and angiosarcoma. A subclass of cancer-associated POT1 mutations actively elongates telomeres (PMID 40015989).

protein_function: odr-4 GPCR localization factor homolog (formerly C1orf27), a membrane-associated accessory protein predicted to be involved in protein localization, specifically trafficking of certain G-protein-coupled receptors (notably odorant receptors) to the cell surface.
gbm_evidence: None found. No glioma or glioblastoma literature on ODR4 exists. The NCBI Gene record carries only predicted annotations - 'Predicted to be involved in protein localization' and 'Predicted to be located in membrane' - with no cancer associations listed; its only disease cross-reference is to the ALS Online Database. Source: https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/gene/54953
subtype_link: None found. INT has no single defining programme, so subtype-specificity is not assessable, but here there is not even a programme to assign: ODR4 belongs to GPCR biogenesis/trafficking, which has no documented connection to any GBM transcriptional subtype. It is not INT-specific and is not linked to any GBM programme at all. Its presence on a target list is most likely a statistical artefact of the selection method rather than a biological signal.
druggable: None known. No inhibitor, drug or tool compound targeting ODR4 was found. Approval status: none known. There is no reported structure-guided or chemical-biology programme on this protein.
cancer_relevance: None found. Searches returned only generic database entries (Human Protein Atlas expression summaries, a COSMIC somatic-mutation page listing passenger-level mutations) with no functional cancer study. ODR4 is essentially unstudied in oncology.
drug_detail: None known. No inhibitor, drug or tool compound targeting ODR4 was found. Approval status: none known. There is no reported structure-guided or chemical-biology programme on this protein.

protein_function: O-phosphoseryl-tRNA:selenocysteinyl-tRNA synthase, the terminal enzyme of selenocysteine biosynthesis, which converts O-phosphoseryl-tRNA(Sec) into selenocysteinyl-tRNA(Sec) and is therefore required for synthesis of all selenoproteins (including GPX4 and the thioredoxin reductases).
gbm_evidence: None found. No glioma or glioblastoma study of SEPSECS was located. The Atlas of Genetics and Cytogenetics in Oncology entry for SEPSECS explicitly classifies it as a 'Non-annotated gene' with respect to cancer and flags its content as 'Preliminary data'; its cited references concern neurological disease (pontocerebellar hypoplasia type 2D, early-onset epileptic encephalopathy, progressive cerebellar atrophy) rather than malignancy. Source: https://atlasgeneticsoncology.org/gene/56393/sepsecs
subtype_link: None found. INT has no single defining programme, so subtype-specificity is not assessable; SEPSECS belongs to selenocysteine/selenoprotein biosynthesis and redox-homeostasis metabolism, with no documented link to any GBM transcriptional subtype and no basis for calling it INT-specific.
druggable: None known specific to SEPSECS. No inhibitor, drug or tool compound targeting SEPSECS was confirmed. Approval status: none known. Adjacent selenoprotein-pathway targets are being explored (e.g. GPX4 inhibitors such as RSL3 and ML210 for ferroptosis induction, and auranofin against thioredoxin reductase), but these act on downstream selenoproteins, not on SEPSECS itself, and should not be credited to this gene.
cancer_relevance: Minimal and only by pathway association. The selenocysteine machinery has cancer relevance - a sibling component, SEPHS2, is over-expressed in triple-negative breast cancer, and 'Selenoproteins and tRNA-Sec: regulators of cancer redox homeostasis' reviews the pathway's role in tumour redox balance - but no primary evidence implicates SEPSECS itself as a cancer gene or dependency.
drug_detail: None known specific to SEPSECS. No inhibitor, drug or tool compound targeting SEPSECS was confirmed. Approval status: none known. Adjacent selenoprotein-pathway targets are being explored (e.g. GPX4 inhibitors such as RSL3 and ML210 for ferroptosis induction, and auranofin against thioredoxin reductase), but these act on downstream selenoproteins, not on SEPSECS itself, and should not be credited to this gene.

protein_function: Adenomatous polyposis coli, a large scaffold protein that forms the beta-catenin destruction complex with AXIN, GSK3beta and CK1 to drive beta-catenin phosphorylation and degradation, thereby switching off canonical Wnt signalling; it also binds microtubules and regulates mitotic spindle and cell migration.
gbm_evidence: Weak, and importantly NEGATIVE for the specific GBM link. Turcot syndrome is the classic APC-brain-tumour association, but the tumour type matters: StatPearls states 'Medulloblastomas are associated with APC gene mutations', whereas 'Glioblastomas are associated with MMR gene mutations, specifically, in the hMLH1 DNA mismatch repair gene'. In other words, APC germline mutation (Turcot type 2) predisposes to MEDULLOBLASTOMA, and the glioblastoma arm of Turcot syndrome (type 1) is driven by mismatch-repair genes, NOT APC. Somatic APC mutation is not a recurrent event in adult GBM. Wnt/beta-catenin signalling is broadly implicated in glioma progression (e.g. 'Wnt3a mediated activation of Wnt/beta-catenin signaling promotes tumor progression in glioblastoma'), but that is pathway-level evidence, not APC-level. Sources: https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK534782/ ; https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S104474311300002X
subtype_link: None found, and there is a MISMATCH on two counts. First, INT has no single defining programme so subtype-specificity is not assessable; APC's programme is canonical Wnt/beta-catenin regulation, with no evidence of enrichment in an intermediate GBM state. Second and more seriously, the GBM-relevant Turcot arm is mismatch-repair-driven, so assigning APC to a glioblastoma target list on the strength of the Turcot association would be a misattribution.
druggable: FLAG - WRONG THERAPEUTIC DIRECTION. APC is one of the archetypal TUMOUR SUPPRESSORS. It functions to DEGRADE beta-catenin and switch OFF Wnt signalling ('The APC tumor suppressor counteracts beta-catenin activation and H3K4 methylation at Wnt target genes', PMID 16510874); biallelic loss causes familial adenomatous polyposis and initiates the majority of sporadic colorectal cancers. Inhibiting APC would ACTIVATE Wnt/beta-catenin signalling and is therefore oncogenic, not therapeutic. No APC inhibitor exists and none should be sought. The correct direction in APC-deficient tumours is inhibition of downstream Wnt output (tankyrase inhibitors, porcupine inhibitors, beta-catenin/TCF disruptors) - all preclinical or early clinical, none approved. Approval status for APC itself: none known, and inhibition is contraindicated in principle.
cancer_relevance: Extensive, as a tumour suppressor. Germline APC loss causes familial adenomatous polyposis and Turcot syndrome type 2; somatic biallelic APC inactivation is the initiating event in roughly 80 percent of sporadic colorectal cancers and is also found in desmoid tumours and hepatoblastoma.
drug_detail: FLAG - WRONG THERAPEUTIC DIRECTION. APC is one of the archetypal TUMOUR SUPPRESSORS. It functions to DEGRADE beta-catenin and switch OFF Wnt signalling ('The APC tumor suppressor counteracts beta-catenin activation and H3K4 methylation at Wnt target genes', PMID 16510874); biallelic loss causes familial adenomatous polyposis and initiates the majority of sporadic colorectal cancers. Inhibiting APC would ACTIVATE Wnt/beta-catenin signalling and is therefore oncogenic, not therapeutic. No APC inhibitor exists and none should be sought. The correct direction in APC-deficient tumours is inhibition of downstream Wnt output (tankyrase inhibitors, porcupine inhibitors, beta-catenin/TCF disruptors) - all preclinical or early clinical, none approved. Approval status for APC itself: none known, and inhibition is contraindicated in principle.
wrong_direction: TUMOUR SUPPRESSOR. Degrades beta-catenin and switches OFF Wnt signalling; biallelic loss causes familial adenomatous polyposis. Inhibiting it would activate Wnt, the opposite of what is wanted.

protein_function: Zinc finger protein 36 like 1 (BRF1/TIS11b), a tristetraprolin-family CCCH tandem zinc-finger RNA-binding protein that binds AU-rich elements in target mRNA 3' UTRs and recruits deadenylases to trigger their degradation.
gbm_evidence: None found for ZFP36L1 itself. The glioblastoma paper in this family concerns the PARALOG ZFP36/TTP - 'ZFP36 expression impairs glioblastoma cell lines viability and invasiveness by targeting multiple signal transduction pathways' (Cell Cycle 2012, PMID 22544323) - which is a different gene and should not be credited to ZFP36L1. Reported honestly as no ZFP36L1-specific GBM evidence.
subtype_link: None found, with a directional caveat. INT has no single defining programme so subtype-specificity is not assessable; ZFP36L1 belongs to post-transcriptional mRNA-decay control of inflammatory, hypoxia and cell-cycle transcripts. Note that this programme is if anything MES-flavoured (AU-rich-element control of inflammatory cytokines) rather than intermediate, so the INT assignment is not supported. Additionally, the paralog data in GBM show ZFP36-family activity SUPPRESSES viability and invasiveness, i.e. the family acts as a brake.
druggable: None known, and inhibition would likely be the wrong direction. No inhibitor, drug or tool compound targeting ZFP36L1 was found. Approval status: none known. RNA-binding proteins of this class remain largely chemically intractable, and since the published role is tumour-suppressive, restoration rather than inhibition would be the rational direction.
cancer_relevance: Yes, and predominantly tumour-suppressive. 'RNA-Binding Protein ZFP36L1 Suppresses Hypoxia and Cell-Cycle Signaling' (Cancer Research 2020, PMID 31551365) establishes a growth-restraining role; the tristetraprolin family is reviewed as a group of tumour suppressors in 'The Tristetraprolin Family of RNA-Binding Proteins in Cancer' (Cancers 2020). ZFP36L1 also has an established role in lymphocyte development.
drug_detail: None known, and inhibition would likely be the wrong direction. No inhibitor, drug or tool compound targeting ZFP36L1 was found. Approval status: none known. RNA-binding proteins of this class remain largely chemically intractable, and since the published role is tumour-suppressive, restoration rather than inhibition would be the rational direction.

protein_function: JAZF zinc finger 1 (TIP27), a nuclear zinc-finger protein that acts as a transcriptional corepressor of the orphan nuclear receptor NR2C2/TR4 and has reported roles in lipid and glucose metabolism.
gbm_evidence: None found. Targeted searches for JAZF1 in glioma/glioblastoma returned no primary study. A review of gene fusions in malignant glioma was retrieved but does not establish JAZF1 fusions in glioma; the Human Protein Atlas cancer page provides expression data only, with no glioma prognostic claim. Reported honestly as no GBM evidence.
subtype_link: None found. INT has no single defining programme, so subtype-specificity is not assessable; JAZF1 belongs to nuclear-receptor transcriptional corepression and metabolic regulation. There is no documented connection to any GBM subtype and no basis for calling it INT-specific.
druggable: None known. No inhibitor, drug or tool compound targeting JAZF1 was confirmed. Approval status: none known. One indirect angle exists - 'JAZF1: A Metabolic Regulator of Sensitivity to a Polyamine-Targeted Therapy' (Mol Cancer Res 2023) positions JAZF1 as a biomarker of response to polyamine-pathway therapy rather than as a direct drug target.
cancer_relevance: Yes, but confined to a specific sarcoma context. JAZF1 is the 5' partner of the recurrent JAZF1-SUZ12 (JJAZ1) fusion that defines low-grade endometrial stromal sarcoma - 'Frequent fusion of the JAZF1 and JJAZ1 genes in endometrial stromal tumors' (PNAS 2001) - with JAZF1-PHF1 and other variants also described. This is a fusion-driven mechanism in a mesenchymal uterine tumour and does not transfer to wild-type JAZF1 in glioma. GWAS also link JAZF1 to type 2 diabetes and prostate cancer risk.
drug_detail: None known. No inhibitor, drug or tool compound targeting JAZF1 was confirmed. Approval status: none known. One indirect angle exists - 'JAZF1: A Metabolic Regulator of Sensitivity to a Polyamine-Targeted Therapy' (Mol Cancer Res 2023) positions JAZF1 as a biomarker of response to polyamine-pathway therapy rather than as a direct drug target.

protein_function: Secreted C1q/TNF-related protein 4 (CTRP4), a two-C1q-domain adipokine/cytokine that signals through nucleolin and modulates NF-kB and STAT3 pathways.
gbm_evidence: none found
subtype_link: Partial and neural rather than oligodendrocytic. Human Protein Atlas classifies C1QTNF4 as tissue-enriched (Brain), protein detected in astrocytes and subsets of neurons. In CNS disease models CTRP4 signalling ameliorates autoimmune encephalomyelitis by suppressing Th17 differentiation. No oligodendrocyte- or myelin-specific evidence found.
druggable: No small-molecule inhibitor known. Recombinant CTRP4 protein is used as a preclinical agonist tool. Approval status: none known.
cancer_relevance: Limited: identified as a cytokine that stimulates STAT3 and NF-kB and promotes cell survival in human cancer cells. No glioma-specific work located.
drug_detail: No small-molecule inhibitor known. Recombinant CTRP4 protein is used as a preclinical agonist tool. Approval status: none known.

protein_function: Mitochondrial phosphatidylserine decarboxylase, an inner-membrane enzyme converting phosphatidylserine to phosphatidylethanolamine, supplying the PE required for cristae architecture.
gbm_evidence: none found. IMPORTANT NEGATIVE: the 2026 paper on targeting phosphatidylserine synthesis in oesophageal carcinoma and glioblastoma (PMID 42511570) concerns PTDSS1, a different enzyme, not PISD. Do not attribute that GBM finding to PISD.
subtype_link: none found for the OLIGO programme. No myelin, oligodendrocyte or CNS-ECM evidence located. PISD is a mitochondrial enzyme, so its biology fits the MTC subtype better than OLIGO - a possible subtype-assignment mismatch worth flagging.
druggable: No selective PISD inhibitor confirmed. Approval status: none known.
cancer_relevance: Moderate: targeting mitochondrial phosphatidylethanolamine alters mitochondrial metabolism and proliferation in hepatocellular carcinoma; PISD promotes ferroptosis through STAT3/GPX4 in gastric cancer.
drug_detail: No selective PISD inhibitor confirmed. Approval status: none known.
subtype_mismatch: Mitochondrial enzyme — biology fits MTC, not OLIGO.
tier: TIER 2 · credible target, no drug yet

protein_function: p150Glued, the largest subunit of the dynactin complex, linking cargo to cytoplasmic dynein for retrograde microtubule transport; mutations cause ALS, Perry syndrome and distal SMA.
gbm_evidence: Glioma but not GBM, and directionally unhelpful. Technol Cancer Res Treat 2021 (PMID 33896271): 'high expressions of DCTN1, DCTN3, DCTN4, and DCTN6 were significantly (P<0.05) related to the favorable OS of LGG patients'. High expression predicting BETTER survival argues against DCTN1 being an oncogenic dependency.
subtype_link: Partial: dynactin/p150Glued is essential for neuronal axonal transport and is a bona fide CNS/neurodegeneration gene. Neural biology, but no oligodendrocyte-, myelin- or CNS-ECM-specific role found.
druggable: No direct dynactin/DCTN1 inhibitor confirmed. Ciliobrevin and dynapyrazole inhibit cytoplasmic dynein, not DCTN1, and are preclinical tool compounds only. Approval status: none known.
cancer_relevance: Limited to the LGG prognostic association above; no functional oncogenic study located.
drug_detail: No direct dynactin/DCTN1 inhibitor confirmed. Ciliobrevin and dynapyrazole inhibit cytoplasmic dynein, not DCTN1, and are preclinical tool compounds only. Approval status: none known.
wrong_direction: In low-grade glioma HIGH expression predicts BETTER survival, which argues against it being an oncogenic dependency.

protein_function: Hyaluronan and proteoglycan link protein 2 (Bral1), a CNS-restricted link protein that stabilises hyaluronan-lectican complexes forming the perinodal extracellular matrix at nodes of Ranvier in myelinated fibres.
gbm_evidence: Database-level only. Human Protein Atlas TCGA analysis classifies HAPLN2 RNA as 'Cancer enriched (Glioblastoma Multiforme)'; however the same resource states HAPLN2 is not prognostic in any cancer. No mechanistic GBM or glioma study was found.
subtype_link: Strong - the best subtype-biology match in the OLIGO list. HAPLN2 preferentially localises with versican at nodes of Ranvier, is essential for nodal ECM formation and interacts with the nodal protein NF186 directly; in Hapln2-null mice there were no ECM signals at CNS nodes. This is precisely myelinated-axon / CNS extracellular-matrix biology.
druggable: None known - a secreted structural ECM link protein with no reported inhibitor, drug or tool compound. Approval status: none known.
cancer_relevance: Essentially none. The literature is dominated by neurodegeneration - aggregation in Parkinson's models, and HAPLN2 aggregates promoting microglial inflammation during brain ageing.
drug_detail: None known - a secreted structural ECM link protein with no reported inhibitor, drug or tool compound. Approval status: none known.
tier: TIER 2 · credible target, no drug yet

protein_function: Mitoferrin-2, an inner mitochondrial membrane carrier importing ferrous iron into the matrix for heme biosynthesis and iron-sulfur cluster assembly.
gbm_evidence: none found. Informative negative: in a diffuse glioma iron-regulatory gene signature study, SLC25A28 was among the 61 genes screened but was excluded by feature selection and is NOT in the final 8-gene survival model.
subtype_link: none found for the OLIGO programme. A mitochondrial carrier, so like PISD its biology fits MTC better than OLIGO; possible subtype-assignment mismatch. The one CNS study found is microglial, not oligodendrocytic.
druggable: No inhibitor or tool compound known. Approval status: none known.
cancer_relevance: Good genetic rationale: 'Mitoferrin2 is a synthetic lethal target for chromosome 8p deleted cancers' (Genome Medicine 2024) - cells that lose the 8p paralog SLC25A37 become dependent on SLC25A28. Also implicated in ferroptosis regulation.
drug_detail: No inhibitor or tool compound known. Approval status: none known.
subtype_mismatch: Mitochondrial iron carrier — biology fits MTC, not OLIGO.
tier: TIER 2 · credible target, no drug yet

protein_function: Ataxin-7-like 3, the obligate adaptor subunit of the SAGA deubiquitination module that activates USP22 to remove monoubiquitin from histone H2B.
gbm_evidence: none found
subtype_link: none found. Chromatin/transcription biology; no myelin, oligodendrocyte or CNS-ECM link reported.
druggable: Indirectly, via its partner enzyme. No direct ATXN7L3 ligand exists, but selective USP22 inhibitors have been reported from structure-based virtual screening with anti-tumour activity in vitro. Approval status: preclinical only.
cancer_relevance: Solid: 'ATXN7L3 and ENY2 Coordinate Activity of Multiple H2B Deubiquitinases Important for Cellular Proliferation and Tumor Growth' (Molecular Cell 2016). Its partner USP22 is a well-studied oncology target.
drug_detail: targetable indirectly through USP22 inhibitors, preclinical only.

protein_function: Ataxin-10, a cytoplasmic armadillo-repeat protein required for cerebellar neuron survival, implicated in cytokinesis and ciliogenesis; an intronic repeat expansion causes SCA10.
gbm_evidence: none found
subtype_link: Weak and generic neural only. No oligodendrocyte, myelin or CNS-ECM evidence found.
druggable: None known. Approval status: none known.
cancer_relevance: none found. ATXN10 appeared only incidentally within a multi-omic IDH-mutant glioma recurrence-prediction feature set, which is not evidence of a biological role.
drug_detail: None known. Approval status: none known.

protein_function: Anillin, an actin-binding scaffold that organises the actomyosin contractile ring during cytokinesis and links septins, F-actin and RhoA; also required for septin assembly in non-dividing myelinating oligodendrocytes.
gbm_evidence: No dedicated glioma or GBM functional study found. Human Protein Atlas reports ANLN is NOT prognostic in glioma (prognostic only in cervical, liver, lung, pancreatic and renal cancer), and GBM mass-spectrometry data were non-significant.
subtype_link: Strong and direct. eLife 2019: 'expression of the cytoskeletal adaptor protein ANLN is strongly enriched in mature oligodendrocytes', Anln mRNA is highest in myelinating oligodendrocytes, and oligodendrocyte-specific knockout causes numerous myelin outfoldings with a 15.5% reduction in nerve conduction velocity. A textbook myelin/oligodendrocyte gene.
druggable: No direct ANLN inhibitor or tool compound found. Approval status: none known.
cancer_relevance: Extensive outside the CNS: prognostic and functionally oncogenic in breast, gallbladder, oral squamous, liver, lung, pancreatic and renal cancers. It is essentially a proliferation-index gene, which sits awkwardly with a differentiated oligodendrocytic programme.
drug_detail: No direct ANLN inhibitor or tool compound found. Approval status: none known.
tier: TIER 2 · credible target, no drug yet

protein_function: Mitochondrial complex I assembly factor that acts with NDUFAF4 to build the Q-module of NADH:ubiquinone oxidoreductase; biallelic mutations cause fatal neonatal mitochondrial disease and cavitating leukoencephalopathy.
gbm_evidence: none found. Human Protein Atlas: prognostic in renal cancer (KICH) only; GBM protein data non-significant.
subtype_link: none found for the OLIGO programme in the sense required. NDUFAF3 is an OXPHOS/complex I gene and is therefore MTC-consistent rather than OLIGO-consistent - a subtype-assignment mismatch worth flagging. The only white-matter connection is that NDUFAF3 variants may associate with cavitating leukoencephalopathy, a secondary consequence of complex I failure rather than a myelin-programme role.
druggable: No NDUFAF3-specific inhibitor exists. Complex I itself is druggable: IACS-010759 is a selective complex I inhibitor that entered phase I trials in advanced solid tumours and AML, though those trials reported dose-limiting neurotoxicity and lactic acidosis; metformin is a weak complex I inhibitor. Approval status: none approved for this indication.
cancer_relevance: Weak gene-specific evidence. Complex I dependency as a class is well established in OXPHOS-high tumours.
drug_detail: IACS-010759, a complex I inhibitor, entered phase I but reported dose-limiting neurotoxicity and lactic acidosis.
subtype_mismatch: Complex I assembly factor — biology fits MTC, not OLIGO.

protein_function: TSPY-like 5, a nucleosome-assembly-protein-family member that binds the deubiquitinase USP7 and thereby suppresses p53 protein levels and function; itself frequently silenced by promoter hypermethylation.
gbm_evidence: Modest and descriptive. EANO/Neuro-Oncology 2017 abstract on CRISPR targeting of the TSPYL family: TSPYL4 and TSPYL5 showed lower expression in brain tumours than normal brain, and the GBM methylome showed a general increase in methylation at TSPYL loci; the authors note their knockouts showed only a 'mild' effect.
subtype_link: none found. No myelin, oligodendrocyte or CNS-ECM evidence located.
druggable: No direct TSPYL5 ligand. The TSPYL5-USP7-p53 axis is indirectly addressable with USP7 inhibitors, which are preclinical. Approval status: none known.
cancer_relevance: Well studied and context-dependent - oncogene in some settings, tumour suppressor in others: TSPYL5 suppresses p53 via USP7 (Nat Cell Biol 2011); silenced by promoter methylation in gastric cancer; inhibits proliferation in colorectal cancer. This bidirectionality is a real liability for target selection.
drug_detail: No direct TSPYL5 ligand. The TSPYL5-USP7-p53 axis is indirectly addressable with USP7 inhibitors, which are preclinical. Approval status: none known.
tier: TIER 2 · credible target, no drug yet
